messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 58
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Product Manager
- Trauma Type: Torture
- Pcl5: 55

He is a 58-year-old South Asian man who has spent most of his adult life learning how to anticipate problems before they happen. In his work as a product manager, that habit has made him successful. He is known for thinking three steps ahead, for staying calm in meetings, for noticing risk early and building systems around it. It is only over time, in the quiet detail of several conversations, that it becomes clear how much of this vigilance began somewhere else.

In his early thirties, before immigrating, he is detained by state authorities during a period of political unrest in his home country. He is not a political leader, but he has attended meetings, signed his name to public statements, and helped circulate information that is considered dangerous. He tells the story carefully at first, as though reading from a document he has edited too many times. Men come for him at night. He remembers his wife standing in the doorway in her nightclothes, asking where they are taking him, and one of the men telling her not to speak. He remembers the ride more than the building itself: the smell of diesel, dirty fabric over his face, his wrists bound too tightly.

What happens over the next several days returns to him in fragments rather than sequence. He is beaten, deprived of sleep, threatened with harm to his family, and forced to remain in painful positions until his body shakes uncontrollably. He says the worst part is not always the pain. It is the deliberate unpredictability. Footsteps in the hall come to mean anything. A door opening makes his stomach drop. Sometimes they question him; sometimes they leave him alone in darkness long enough that he starts talking to himself just to hear a human voice. He becomes convinced that if he lets himself relax, even for a second, something worse will happen.

He is eventually released through family intervention, but release does not feel like safety. For months afterward he startles at every sound outside the apartment. When someone knocks at the door unexpectedly, he feels heat rush through his body and has to fight the urge to hide. He does not tell his wife much. He says only that they should leave if they can. They immigrate a few years later, and to everyone around them the move looks like a story of perseverance and opportunity.

He builds a life in the United States with discipline and relentless effort. He studies, changes fields, and settles into the technology industry. He marries his ambition to routine. He wakes early, checks locks, reviews schedules, and finds comfort in contingency plans. At work, people describe him as meticulous, maybe overly so. He prefers conference rooms where he can see the door. He dislikes being approached from behind and feels irritated when younger colleagues clap him on the shoulder in celebration. If a meeting becomes tense, especially with raised male voices, he stops hearing the content and begins tracking exits, posture, tone. He tells himself this is just professionalism, just reading the room.

For many years he keeps the past partitioned. He does not watch films about prisons or political violence. He avoids news from his home country, though he scans headlines compulsively during periods of unrest and then cannot sleep after. His wife knows there are places inside him she cannot reach. She has long since stopped asking why he patrols the house at night after a noise, or why he insists on sitting at the edge in restaurants, facing outward. Their children grow up knowing that Baba does not like surprises and should not be awakened abruptly.

What brings everything closer to the surface is not one event but an accumulation. A corporate reorganization puts him under a younger executive whose management style is domineering and erratic. Last-minute demands, hostile questioning in meetings, and late-night messages begin to unsettle him in a way he does not understand at first. Then a colleague jokes during a team exercise by blindfolding volunteers, and he feels his chest clamp so suddenly that he has to leave the room. After that, the boundary between then and now seems thinner. He begins waking at 3 a.m., drenched in sweat, with the clear sensation that someone is standing over him. Some mornings he sits in his car in the office parking lot unable to make himself go inside.

He is ashamed of how frightened he feels. He is also angry—at his boss, at himself, sometimes at his wife when she asks simple questions at the wrong moment. He notices that he has become more withdrawn at home. His grandchildren’s squealing play, once joyful, can suddenly feel piercing. Crowded grocery stores exhaust him. He scans faces without meaning to. On especially bad days, he loses time staring at a spreadsheet while his mind replays a corridor, a hand on his neck, the sound of boots approaching. He knows these are memories, but his body does not seem to know.

By the time he speaks more openly, he says he is tired of living as though danger is always about to step through the door. He has a good marriage, a respected career, and a life he once hoped for, yet much of each day is still organized around avoiding reminders, controlling uncertainty, and recovering from waves of fear that arrive before thought. What is striking is how long he has carried this alone, and how much of his life has been shaped by surviving something he rarely names aloud.
